cim: AI cheating in exams — How Artificial Intelligence is Breaking Traditional Testing
cim_eredeti: AI cheating in exams — How Artificial Intelligence is Breaking Traditional Testing
szoveg_eredeti:
Recently, one of the hottest issues heating up Korean society is cheating in examinations using artificial intelligence (AI). The controversy began when a top scorer on the tax accountant exam confessed to using a ultra-small camera and AI to cheat, and it quickly spread to the Legal Aptitude Test (LEET) and the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT). It even led to a tragic incident where a perfect scorer on the LEET, who had been facing AI cheating allegations, was found dead after giving notice of a public verification to prove his actual skills.

As the controversy spread, the government announced countermeasures such as strengthening the management of returned smart devices and blocking communications within test centers. Videos showing exam questions being solved using AI glasses appeared on YouTube, and search volumes for related devices surged on secondhand trading platforms.

Of course, strengthening supervision to prevent exam cheating is necessary. Ensuring that people who prepared for exams honestly do not suffer unfair damage is a fundamental role of the testing system. However, the method of finding and banning new technologies and tightening supervision every time a new technology emerges seems to have its limitations.

Another question that arose while encountering this crisis was what examinations should actually evaluate. In an era where AI searches for information faster than humans and even solves complex problems, we need to think about whether it is still appropriate to judge an individual’s capabilities solely on how many correct answers they know.

Traditionally, exams evaluated individual abilities centered on how many questions could be solved accurately within a limited time. The ability to hit the correct answer was an important criterion for measuring knowledge and understanding. However, now AI instantly provides answers based on massive amounts of information. The act of finding correct answers itself is no longer an ability exclusive to humans.

Moving forward, the ability to independently solve given problems will become much more important. This goes beyond simply knowing the answer to accurately grasping what the problem is, finding and analyzing necessary information, and deriving solutions based on one’s own judgment.

In reality, the problems encountered in real life often do not have fixed answers like test papers. Multiple solutions exist for the same situation, and which choice is most appropriate varies depending on the given conditions and environment. What is needed at this time is not the ability to pull out memorized answers, but the judgment to understand the situation, compare various possibilities, and make reasonable decisions.

The answers presented by AI are not always correct either. Information may be inaccurate or fail to adequately reflect real-world conditions. Rather than accepting AI’s answers as they are, the ability to find errors and review them based on one’s knowledge and experience is crucial. How accurately one understands and utilizes the results, rather than how proficiently one uses the technology, can become the benchmark dividing individual capability.

Such changes also cast new questions on examination methods. Moving beyond evaluations that select a single correct answer, approaches that examine the reasoning behind a conclusion or how solutions are adjusted when given conditions change could also become possible.

This AI cheating controversy revealed the vulnerabilities of existing testing systems. At the same time, it made us look back at what kind of capabilities humans need in an era of rapid technological advancement. Preventing cheating is important, but I think deliberations on what exams exist to verify must also take place together.

The purpose of an exam will likely not be limited to screening out people who get the most correct answers. Checking whether the knowledge and abilities possessed by individuals can actually be applied in real-life situations is also important.

Now, what exams must ask is not how many correct answers one knows, but how deeply one understands a given problem and can solve it with one’s own strength.
